edits.old:
### 5. What would have to be true for parity at 10–25 Mpts/s and 200–300 m

This subsection turns the budget around and asks what FMCW would need to match ToF. Parity needs all five conditions below. Items 1–3 are engineering, item 4 is physics-limited (§C10.3a) and item 5 is commercial.

1. SOA/laser wall-plug **≥30% at 105 °C**, with ≥100 mW per channel on SiN or III-V waveguides.
2. A stacked or monolithic electronic-photonic receiver at **≈8–13 mW per channel**, i.e. ≈2–3 mW for each of its four receivers, including 1 GS/s ADCs and FFT (§C7b subsection 5).
3. Integrated sub-100 kHz lasers with ≤$10^{-4}$ chirp nonlinearity, qualified to automotive grade.
4. An architecture that restores coverage, i.e. many spatial modes per sample so that each sample sees its whole cell rather than ≈2% of it (§C10.3b, Result 2), without multiplying channels.
5. Volume: a program in the hundreds of thousands per year to run the cost curve.
edits.new:
### 5. What parity would need: the three conditions of §C7b subsection 5

This subsection summarizes the parity arithmetic of §C7b subsection 5. Parity means ≥15 Mpts/s in ≤15 W at 200 m on a 10% target, which leaves 0.8 µJ of electricity per point after the 3 W overhead (Eq. (123)); the 2026 SPAD ToF model meets it with $3+15\times0.415=9.2$ W. The central 2026 FMCW model needs 4.90 µJ per point, i.e. $3+15\times4.90=76.5$ W at 15 Mpts/s. Three conditions must land together; any two of them alone leave a 15 Mpts/s sensor at ≈23.5 W or more (§C7b subsection 5 table).

1. **A low-power coherent receiver chip**, with the electronics and photonics stacked or monolithic: ≈2–3 mW per receiver including ≈1 GS/s ADCs and FFT, i.e. ≈0.10 µJ of receiver energy per point against the model's 2.34 µJ, for 115–190 channels of four receivers each.
2. **CW lasers and amplifiers at ≥30% wall-plug efficiency at 105 °C**, twice the model's 15%.
3. **≈0.15 µJ of optical energy per point** at 200 m, half the model's 0.30 µJ, which needs a receive efficiency $\eta$ near 0.5, or more looks per point, each with its own receiver.

With all three and the model's ungated dwell (10 µs of integration, so 15 mW per channel and 190 channels), a point costs $0.150\times1.267/0.30+0.10=0.73$ µJ, and a 15 Mpts/s sensor draws $3+15\times0.73=14.0$ W: just inside the target, yet still 1.8× the electrical energy per point of the SPAD ToF model ($0.73/0.415$). Channels brighter than ≈22 mW stay inside 15 W only with a gated transmitter: at 30 mW per channel the sensor draws 16 W ungated and 12 W gated (§C7b subsection 5). More power per channel is not a lever: it trades receivers against light wasted during the round trips, and the optimum is already ≈30–40 mW per channel (§C7b subsection 2(h)). The energies also assume a laser narrow enough to lose little to phase noise: ≲27 kHz for a 1 dB coherent loss at 200 m, or ≲55 kHz for 3 dB at 300 m (Eq. (115); table in §C7b subsection 2(e)), with its residual chirp error inside Eq. (112), all qualified to automotive grade. Two gaps lie outside this per-watt definition: each sample covers only ≈2% of its cell (§C10.3b, Result 2), which more modes per sample would close at the price of more receivers (§C7b subsection 6, item 3), and the cost curve needs programs of hundreds of thousands of units a year (subsection 4).
edits.why: Parity follows §C7b subsection 5 (three conditions at 200 m); the ≥100 mW condition is dropped; linewidth restated from Eq. (115).
